Mechanics.question: If the net force on an object is zero, the object must be at rest.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. According to Newton's First Law, if the net force is zero, the object's velocity is constant. This means it can be at rest OR moving at a constant velocity.

Mechanics.question: Momentum is a scalar quantity.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. Momentum (p = mv) is a vector quantity. It has both magnitude and direction, which is the same as the direction of the velocity.

Mechanics.question: The work done by a centripetal force on an object moving in a circle is always zero.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the direction of the object's instantaneous velocity (displacement). Since Work = Fd cos(θ) and θ = 90°, the work done is zero.

Mechanics.question: When a non-elastic collision occurs, both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. In a non-elastic (or inelastic) collision, total momentum is conserved, but some kinetic energy is converted into other forms, such as heat or sound. Therefore, kinetic energy is not conserved.

Mechanics.question: An object thrown upwards reaches its maximum height when its acceleration is zero.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. At the maximum height, the object's instantaneous velocity is zero, but its acceleration is still the acceleration due to gravity (g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downwards), assuming air resistance is negligible.

Mechanics.question: The period of a satellite in a stable circular orbit around the Earth depends on the mass of the satellite.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. The period of a satellite in a circular orbit depends on the radius of the orbit and the mass of the central body (Earth), but not on the satellite's own mass.

Mechanics.question: Weight is a measure of an object's inertia.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. Mass is the measure of an object's inertia (resistance to change in motion). Weight is the gravitational force acting on that mass (W = mg).

Mechanics.question: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. These two forces act on the same object.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. The action and reaction forces (Newton's Third Law) are equal and opposite, but they act on two different objects. For example, the Earth pulls on the Moon, and the Moon pulls on the Earth.

Mechanics.question: If the speed of an object is doubled, its kinetic energy is also doubled.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. Kinetic energy is given by KE = ½mv². If the speed (v) is doubled, the kinetic energy becomes KE' = ½m(2v)² = 4(½mv²) = 4KE. The kinetic energy is quadrupled.

Mechanics.question: An object is in equilibrium only if it is at rest.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. An object is in equilibrium if the net force and net torque acting on it are zero. This can occur when the object is at rest (static equilibrium) or when it is moving with a constant velocity and constant angular velocity (dynamic equilibrium).

Mechanics.question: The principle of conservation of momentum applies only to collisions in the absence of external forces.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. The total momentum of a system is conserved only if the net external force acting on the system is zero.

Mechanics.question: Work is a vector quantity.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. Work is a scalar quantity, calculated as the dot product of force and displacement vectors (W = F · d). It has magnitude but no direction.

Mechanics.question: The centripetal acceleration of an object in uniform circular motion is directed tangentially.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. The centripetal acceleration is always directed towards the center of the circle, perpendicular to the tangential velocity.

Mechanics.question: Power is the rate at which energy is consumed.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. Power is defined as the rate of doing work or the rate of energy transfer (P = W/t or P = dE/dt).

Mechanics.question: An object with constant speed can have a non-zero acceleration.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. An object in uniform circular motion has a constant speed but is continuously accelerating because its direction of velocity is changing. This is the centripetal acceleration.

Mechanics.question: Friction always opposes the motion of an object.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. Static friction can act in the direction of motion or intended motion. For example, when you walk, the static friction from the ground on your foot pushes you forward.

Mechanics.question: The impulse on an object is equal to the change in its kinetic energy.
Mechanics.explanation: Incorrect. The impulse on an object is equal to the change in its momentum (Impulse = Δp). The work-energy theorem states that the net work done is equal to the change in kinetic energy.

Mechanics.question: In a projectile motion, the horizontal component of velocity remains constant.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. Assuming negligible air resistance, there is no horizontal force acting on the projectile, so its horizontal acceleration is zero and its horizontal velocity is constant.

Mechanics.question: The escape velocity from Earth is the same for a rocket and a feather.
Mechanics.explanation: Correct. The escape velocity depends on the mass and radius of the planet (Earth), not on the mass of the object escaping it.

Mechanics.question: A block is moving at a constant speed under a 12 N pushing force and a 2 N pulling force, against friction. The kinetic friction force is 10 N.
Mechanics.explanation: True. 'Constant speed' means the net force is zero. The total forward force is 12 N - 2 N = 10 N. To balance this, the kinetic friction force must be 10 N in the opposite direction.

Mechanics.question: A block of mass m is held at rest on a smooth incline (angle θ) by a horizontal force F. The magnitude of F is mg sinθ.
Mechanics.explanation: False. The component of weight down the incline is mg sinθ. The component of the horizontal force F up the incline is F cosθ. For equilibrium, F cosθ = mg sinθ, which means F = mg tanθ.

Mechanics.question: On a v-t graph for two cars starting from the same position, the point where their graphs intersect means they are at the same position.
Mechanics.explanation: False. The intersection point means they have the same instantaneous velocity. The areas under their graphs must be equal for them to be at the same position.

Mechanics.question: A car traveling east at 80 km/h changes direction to travel north at 60 km/h. The magnitude of its change in velocity is 100 km/h.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Change in velocity is Δv = v_final - v_initial = (60 N) - (80 E) = (60 N) + (80 W). Using Pythagoras on the vectors, the magnitude is √(60² + 80²) = 100 km/h.

Mechanics.question: Two identical blocks slide from rest down two smooth inclined planes of the same height H but different angles. The block on the steeper incline will reach the bottom with a greater final speed.
Mechanics.explanation: False. By conservation of energy (mgh = ½mv²), the loss in P.E. is the same for both, so their final K.E. and final speed (v) must be identical, regardless of the path.

Mechanics.question: In the scenario above, the time taken to reach the bottom will be the same for both blocks.
Mechanics.explanation: False. The block on the steeper incline experiences a greater acceleration (a = g sinθ) and travels a shorter distance. It will reach the bottom in less time.

Mechanics.question: A 1 kg mass (Y) hanging over a pulley pulls a 0.5 kg mass (X) on a smooth horizontal table. When Y falls 1 m from rest, its final speed can be found using m_Ygh = ½m_Yv².
Mechanics.explanation: False. The potential energy lost by Y (m_Ygh) is converted into the kinetic energy of both masses (X and Y), which move together. The correct equation is m_Ygh = ½m_Yv² + ½m_Xv².

Mechanics.question: A machine lifts a block vertically up at speed v. If it instead pulls it up a smooth incline at the same speed v, the power output required is the same.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Power = Force × velocity. To lift vertically, Force = mg. To pull up a smooth incline, Force = mg sinθ. Since sinθ < 1, the force and thus the power required (P = (mg sinθ)v) are less for the incline.

Mechanics.question: A car's headrest is primarily designed to minimize injury when the car brakes suddenly.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Its main safety function is to prevent whiplash (neck injury) when the car is struck from behind. The headrest supports the head, which by inertia lags behind the rest of the body.

Mechanics.question: When cutting an object with scissors, the cutting force is largest at the tips of the blades and smallest near the pivot.
Mechanics.explanation: False. By the principle of moments (levers), the output force is inversely proportional to the distance from the pivot. The force is largest near the pivot (smallest distance) and smallest at the tips.

Mechanics.question: To find the center of gravity (C.G.) of a non-uniform plate, you suspend it from one vertex (P) and draw a vertical line. The C.G. lies on this line.
Mechanics.explanation: False. This is only the first step. You must then suspend the plate from a second, different point (e.g., Q) and draw a second vertical line. The C.G. is the point where the two lines intersect.

Mechanics.question: When an object falls from rest, the distance it falls in time t is s. The distance it falls in time 2t is 4s.
Mechanics.explanation: True. For an object in free fall from rest, s = ½gt². The distance s is proportional to t². If you double the time t to 2t, the distance becomes proportional to (2t)² = 4t², which is 4s.

Mechanics.question: An object falling from rest travels 9m in time t₁. It then travels another 16m in time t₂. The ratio t₁:t₂ must be 3:4.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Since s ∝ t², the time to travel 9m is t₁ ∝ √9 = 3. The total time to travel (9+16)=25m is (t₁+t₂) ∝ √25 = 5. If t₁ = 3k and (t₁+t₂) = 5k, then t₂ = 2k. The ratio t₁:t₂ is 3:2.

Mechanics.question: For an object starting from rest, the area under its Force-time (F-t) graph represents the work done on it.
Mechanics.explanation: False. The area under an F-t graph is the impulse (which equals the change in momentum, mΔv). The area under a Force-distance (F-s) graph represents the work done.

Mechanics.question: In free fall under gravity, the displacement–time graph is a straight line.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Constant acceleration gives a parabolic displacement–time graph.

Mechanics.question: In free fall under gravity, the velocity–time graph is a straight line with slope −g (taking downward negative).
Mechanics.explanation: True. This represents constant acceleration.

Mechanics.question: Two satellites in circular orbits of the same radius around Earth have the same speed and period, regardless of orbital plane orientation.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Speed and period formulas v = √(GM/R) and T = 2π√(R³/GM) are independent of the plane's orientation.

Mechanics.question: The centripetal force on a satellite is directed along the plane of its orbit, toward the center.
Mechanics.explanation: True. It points toward Earth’s center and lies in the orbital plane.

Mechanics.question: For two cars on a v–t graph starting at the same position, their separation is maximum at the time when the area between their v–t curves (from t = 0) is maximum.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Relative displacement is the time integral of relative velocity.

Mechanics.question: If two cars’ velocities have the same sign over an interval, they travel in the same direction during that interval.
Mechanics.explanation: True. The sign of velocity indicates direction.

Mechanics.question: If one car’s v–t curve lies below the other’s for a long enough time, that car will lag behind in position.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Less positive (or more negative) velocity accumulates less forward displacement.

Mechanics.question: On a banked curve with no friction, the centripetal force equals mg tan θ.
Mechanics.explanation: True. The horizontal component of the normal force provides the centripetal force: N sinθ = (mg/cosθ) sinθ = mg tanθ.

Mechanics.question: In a frictionless banked turn, the normal reaction’s horizontal component provides the centripetal force.
Mechanics.explanation: True. With no friction, only the normal force N can have a horizontal component.

Mechanics.question: A free-body diagram should include a “resultant force” arrow in addition to all actual forces.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Only actual forces are drawn; the resultant is inferred by their vector sum.

Mechanics.question: The change in velocity is the vector difference v_final − v_initial, not the magnitude of the resultant velocity.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Δv is a vector subtraction.

Mechanics.question: An object falling from very far toward an airless planet speeds up with increasing acceleration; its v–t curve is concave upward, not a straight line.
Mechanics.explanation: True. The acceleration a ∝ 1/r² increases as the distance r decreases.

Mechanics.question: Weight and air resistance on a projectile form an action–reaction pair.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Action–reaction pairs act on different bodies; the weight's pair is with the Earth’s pull.

Mechanics.question: Rocket acceleration should be found from a = (F_thrust − mg)/m (ignoring drag).
Mechanics.explanation: True. This is an application of Newton’s second law.

Mechanics.question: For a block at rest on a horizontal surface, the normal reaction R and its weight W are not an action–reaction pair, even though they can be equal and opposite.
Mechanics.explanation: True. Action–reaction pairs must act on different bodies.

Mechanics.question: When the block is in equilibrium on a horizontal surface, R equals W in magnitude.
Mechanics.explanation: True. This is due to the force balance in the vertical direction.

Mechanics.question: A block sliding down a rough incline at constant velocity has zero net force; the resultant force from the incline (normal + friction) balances the component of weight.
Mechanics.explanation: True. This is a condition of zero acceleration.

Mechanics.question: At the highest point of a projectile’s trajectory (neglecting air), its vertical velocity is zero and its speed equals the horizontal component.
Mechanics.explanation: True. At the peak, v_y = 0, so the total speed v = v_x.

Mechanics.question: If forces on a mass are balanced, then it accelerates.
Mechanics.explanation: False. Balanced forces imply zero acceleration.

Mechanics.question: For a perfectly elastic bounce, a ball’s speed just after impact equals its speed just before impact (ignoring air resistance).
Mechanics.explanation: True. An elastic collision with the ground reverses the velocity component normal to the surface without loss of speed.

Mechanics.question: The area under a force–time graph equals the impulse and hence the change in momentum.
Mechanics.explanation: True. This is the impulse–momentum theorem.

Mechanics.question: The slope of a force–time graph gives the acceleration directly.
Mechanics.explanation: False. The slope is dF/dt; acceleration is F/m.

Mechanics.question: For lifting a load steadily from height difference Δh, the work done by the crane equals WΔh regardless of the horizontal path taken.
Mechanics.explanation: True. The work done against gravity depends only on the vertical displacement.

Mechanics.question: The crane’s work on a steady lift depends on the horizontal displacement.
Mechanics.explanation: False. There is no change in gravitational potential from horizontal motion.

Mechanics.question: In a two-mass system connected over a pulley, the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the total kinetic energy gained by both masses (neglecting losses).
Mechanics.explanation: True. This is a statement of energy conservation.

Mechanics.question: A book rests on a table. The book’s weight and the table’s normal reaction

options.B: are equal and opposite forces on the same body (equilibrium pair, not N3)
options.D: only balance if the table is accelerating

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Classic N3 trap (2021). N3 pair: Earth–book gravity and book–Earth.

Mechanics.question: Newton’s third-law action and reaction forces always

options.A: act on the same object and cancel
options.B: act on different objects
options.C: have different magnitudes if masses differ

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Action and reaction act on two different bodies, so they never cancel on the same free-body diagram.

Mechanics.question: A block slides down a rough incline at constant velocity. The net force along the slope is

options.B: zero

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force along the slope is zero (N1).

Mechanics.question: On a v–t graph, two cars’ traces cross. At that instant they necessarily have the same

options.B: velocity

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Intersection = same v; same position needs equal areas.

Mechanics.question: In uniform circular motion, ‘the centripetal force’ is best described as

options.A: a new type of force in addition to weight and tension/friction
options.B: the name for the net force toward the centre provided by real forces
options.D: always equal to friction alone, by definition

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. ‘Centripetal force’ names the net force toward the centre; it is provided by real forces (tension, friction, weight components), not an extra force type.

Mechanics.question: A spring balance measures

options.B: force (often calibrated as weight reading)
options.C: mass in all situations including free fall without caveat

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. A spring balance measures force (often shown as a weight reading), not length in metres.

Mechanics.question: In a freely falling lift (ideal free fall), a beam balance comparing two masses

options.A: reads slightly less than true mass ratio
options.B: reads slightly more
options.C: cannot give the usual ‘weight comparison’ reading because both sides are weightless effectively

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: C. In free fall both pans are effectively weightless, so a beam balance cannot give the usual weight comparison — it is not merely a smaller reading.

Mechanics.question: If forces on a body are balanced (net force zero), the body

options.B: must have zero acceleration (rest or uniform velocity)

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Zero net force means zero acceleration: the body may be at rest or move at constant velocity.

Mechanics.question: For a rocket going straight up, net force is best written as

options.B: thrust + weight

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: C. Taking up as positive, net force = thrust − weight (directions accounted for), not thrust alone.

Mechanics.question: A projectile in flight (ignore air). At the highest point

options.B: velocity is zero
options.C: vertical velocity component is zero; horizontal may be non-zero so KE ≠ 0

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: C. At the top, vertical velocity is zero but horizontal velocity can remain, so speed and KE need not be zero; g still acts.

Mechanics.question: Weight and air resistance on a falling projectile

options.B: both act on the projectile so cannot be a Newton III pair

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. A Newton III pair acts on two different objects; weight and drag both act on the projectile, so they are not a III pair.

Mechanics.question: Kinetic friction on a sliding block

options.A: becomes zero the instant an applied push is removed, even if still sliding
options.B: acts while there is sliding, opposing relative motion
options.C: always equals μN with N = mg on every incline with extra forces
options.D: acts in the direction of velocity

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Kinetic friction acts whenever there is sliding and opposes relative motion; it does not vanish the instant the push is removed if sliding continues.

Mechanics.question: On a free-body diagram for a block on an incline, you should

options.A: draw weight, normal, friction (as needed) — not also ‘mg sinθ’ and ‘resultant’ as extra force arrows on top of mg
options.B: always draw mg sinθ as a separate force in addition to full weight
options.D: draw centripetal force even for straight incline motion

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: A. Draw weight, normal and friction as needed — do not also add mg sinθ or ‘resultant’ as extra force arrows on top of full weight (double-counting).

Mechanics.question: Change in velocity is a

options.B: vector; magnitude by vector subtraction, not |v₂|−|v₁| alone when direction changes

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Δv is a vector; when direction changes you must subtract vectors, not just |v₂| − |v₁|.

Mechanics.question: When a bungee cord first becomes taut

options.A: the jumper must start decelerating immediately
options.B: net force may still be downward if weight > cord force, so downward speed can still increase for a while

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. When the cord first tautens, tension may still be less than weight, so net force can stay downward and speed can keep rising briefly.

Mechanics.question: Area under a force–time graph equals

options.B: impulse (Δp)

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Area under a force–time graph is impulse, equal to change in momentum Δp.

Mechanics.question: Area under a force–displacement graph equals

options.B: work done

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Area under a force–displacement graph is work done (energy transferred by the force).

Mechanics.question: A car headrest’s main safety role in a rear-end collision is to

options.A: reduce injury mainly when braking hard from the front
options.B: support the head to reduce whiplash as the seat pushes the torso forward

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. In a rear-end crash the seat pushes the torso forward; the headrest supports the head to reduce whiplash.

Mechanics.question: On a smooth incline, two paths same height: final speeds from rest (energy)

options.B: same (same loss of PE → same KE if smooth)

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. On a smooth incline only height matters: same PE loss → same KE and final speed; the steeper path just takes less time.

Mechanics.question: For circular motion of a whirling bob on a string, tension

options.A: equals weight + ‘centripetal force’ treated as an extra force object
options.B: is one of the real forces; net of tension (and weight components) toward centre is mv²/r
options.C: is always equal to mv²/r with weight ignored in all geometries

Mechanics.explanation: Correct answer: B. Tension is a real force; the net of tension and weight components toward the centre equals mv²/r — do not treat ‘centripetal force’ as an extra object.

Heat & Gases.question: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct. For an ideal gas, there are no intermolecular forces, so its internal energy is purely the sum of the kinetic energies of its molecules, which is directly proportional to its absolute temperature (U ∝ T).

Heat & Gases.question: During an isothermal expansion of an ideal gas, the gas does no work because its temperature remains constant.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. During an isothermal expansion, the gas does positive work on its surroundings. To keep the temperature constant, heat must be supplied to the gas, according to the first law of thermodynamics (ΔU = Q - W; since ΔU = 0, Q = W).

Heat & Gases.question: When two objects of equal mass but different specific heat capacities and different initial temperatures reach thermal equilibrium, the final temperature will be the simple average of the two initial temperatures.
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. The object with the higher specific heat capacity (c) will undergo a smaller temperature change (since Q = mcΔT). The final temperature will be closer to the initial temperature of the object with the higher heat capacity (C=mc).

Heat & Gases.question: In a vacuum flask, the silvered surfaces are designed to reduce heat transfer by conduction.
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. The vacuum prevents heat transfer by conduction and convection. The silvered surfaces (facing the vacuum) reduce heat transfer by radiation.

Heat & Gases.question: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure (p) plotted against 1/Volume (1/V) will be a curve.
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. Boyle's Law is p ∝ 1/V, or p = k(1/V). This is a direct proportionality (y = mx). A graph of p against 1/V will be a straight line through the origin. A graph of p against V would be the curve.

Heat & Gases.question: Absolute zero (0 Kelvin) is the temperature at which all molecular motion ceases completely.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct. Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature where particles have minimum vibrational motion, representing the minimum possible internal energy. It is the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

Heat & Gases.question: A pressure cooker cooks food faster because it increases the specific heat capacity of water.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. A pressure cooker increases the pressure inside, which raises the boiling point of water. Cooking at a higher temperature (above 100°C) significantly speeds up the chemical reactions in cooking.

Heat & Gases.question: Heat is a measure of how hot an object is.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. Temperature is a measure of how hot an object is (related to the average kinetic energy of its particles). Heat is the energy transferred between objects due to a temperature difference.

Heat & Gases.question: In an adiabatic process, the temperature of the system must remain constant.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. An adiabatic process is one in which no heat is exchanged with the surroundings (Q=0). The temperature can change, for example, during adiabatic compression, the temperature of a gas increases.

Heat & Gases.question: Evaporation is a cooling process.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct. During evaporation, the most energetic molecules escape from the liquid surface, which lowers the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules, thus decreasing the temperature of the liquid.

Heat & Gases.question: Conduction is the primary mode of heat transfer in gases.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. Convection is the primary mode of heat transfer in fluids (liquids and gases). Conduction is the main mode of heat transfer in solids.

Heat & Gases.question: Two objects are in thermal equilibrium if they have the same internal energy.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. Two objects are in thermal equilibrium if they are at the same temperature, meaning there is no net flow of heat between them.

Heat & Gases.question: The specific latent heat of vaporization of a substance is generally smaller than its specific latent heat of fusion.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. The latent heat of vaporization is typically much larger than the latent heat of fusion because a greater amount of energy is required to completely separate the molecules (liquid to gas) than to just loosen their bonds (solid to liquid).

Heat & Gases.question: According to the ideal gas law (PV=nRT), if you double the absolute temperature of a gas while keeping the volume constant, the pressure will be halved.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. According to PV=nRT, if T is doubled and V is constant, the pressure P must also be doubled to maintain the equality.

Heat & Gases.question: A black surface is a good absorber of radiation, but a poor emitter of radiation.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. A good absorber of thermal radiation is also a good emitter of thermal radiation. A perfect black body is a perfect absorber and a perfect emitter.

Heat & Gases.question: When a bimetallic strip is heated, it bends towards the metal with the higher thermal expansion coefficient.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. The metal with the higher coefficient of thermal expansion expands more. To accommodate this greater length, the strip must bend away from it, so it bends towards the metal with the lower coefficient.

Heat & Gases.question: The first law of thermodynamics is a statement of the conservation of energy.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct. The first law (ΔU = Q - W) states that the change in a system's internal energy (ΔU) is equal to the heat added to the system (Q) minus the work done by the system (W), which is a direct application of energy conservation.

Heat & Gases.question: Boiling can occur at any temperature, while evaporation only occurs at a specific boiling point.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. It's the other way around. Evaporation can occur at any temperature from the surface of a liquid, whereas boiling is the bulk vaporization that occurs at a specific temperature (the boiling point) for a given pressure.

Heat & Gases.question: Water has a very low specific heat capacity.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. Water has a very high specific heat capacity compared to most other common substances. This is why it is used as a coolant and why large bodies of water moderate climates.

Heat & Gases.question: Increasing the pressure on ice can cause it to melt, even below 0°C.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct. For water, the solid phase (ice) is less dense than the liquid phase. Increasing the pressure lowers the melting point, a phenomenon called regelation. This is why an ice skate's blade melts the ice beneath it.

Heat & Gases.question: The average kinetic energy of molecules in a gas is proportional to the temperature in degrees Celsius.
Heat & Gases.explanation: Incorrect. The average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to the absolute temperature, which must be measured in Kelvin (K).

Heat & Gases.question: When two equal-mass blocks at 40°C and 30°C are in good thermal contact with no heat loss, and the hotter one has a larger specific heat capacity, the final common temperature is higher than 35°C.
Heat & Gases.explanation: True. Energy balance with equal masses gives Tf closer to the initial temperature of the block with larger c.

Heat & Gases.question: For the situation above, the final temperature is exactly 35°C.
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. Only equal specific heat capacities would yield 35°C; here cX > cY, so Tf > 35°C.

Heat & Gases.question: When mixing water at 50°C with ice at 0°C in an insulated container, the final temperature cannot be below 0°C.
Heat & Gases.explanation: True. The ice–water mixture's temperature is pinned at 0°C until all the ice melts.

Heat & Gases.question: In such a mixture, if insufficient hot water is available to melt all the ice, the final temperature is 0°C.
Heat & Gases.explanation: True. This is due to the phase change plateau.

Heat & Gases.question: The root-mean-square speed of gas molecules scales directly with temperature (v_rms ∝ T).
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. The correct relationship is v_rms ∝ √T.

Heat & Gases.question: In the ideal gas equation, temperature must be in kelvin.
Heat & Gases.explanation: True. The equation requires an absolute temperature scale.

Heat & Gases.question: Gas pressure is due to molecular impacts on the container walls; collisions among molecules themselves do not directly exert pressure on the walls.
Heat & Gases.explanation: True. The momentum transfer at the walls is what defines pressure.

Heat & Gases.question: A good thermal conductor (e.g., copper) necessarily “absorbs more heat” than a poor conductor at the same mass and temperature change.
Heat & Gases.explanation: False. The heat absorbed depends on mcΔT (heat capacity), not on thermal conductivity.

Heat & Gases.question: In a vacuum flask, what is the main purpose of the silvered walls facing the vacuum?

options.B: Reduce heat transfer by convection
options.D: Increase the heat capacity of the flask

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: C. A/B confuse vacuum’s role (stops conduction/convection) with silvering (reflects IR). D invents a capacity change.

Heat & Gases.question: For an ideal gas kept at constant temperature, a graph of pressure p against 1/V is

options.B: a straight line through the origin
options.C: a straight line with negative gradient

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Boyle: p ∝ 1/V. A is what students draw for p–V. C mixes Charles/Gay-Lussac shapes.

Heat & Gases.question: The pressure of an ideal gas on the walls of a container is mainly due to

options.B: collisions of molecules with the walls

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. A is the classic misconception flagged in reports. C/D not kinetic-theory pressure.

Heat & Gases.question: When using pV = nRT, temperature must be in

options.B: kelvin

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. In pV = nRT, T must be absolute thermodynamic temperature in kelvin, not °C.

Heat & Gases.question: Two objects of equal mass but different specific heat capacities start at different temperatures and reach thermal equilibrium. The final temperature is

options.A: always the arithmetic mean of the two initial temperatures
options.B: closer to the initial T of the object with larger heat capacity mc
options.C: closer to the initial T of the object with smaller c

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Equal mass ≠ equal share of ΔT. Q = mcΔT → larger C means smaller |ΔT|.

Heat & Gases.question: A good thermal conductor (e.g. copper) compared with a poor conductor of the same mass and same ΔT

options.B: always absorbs less thermal energy
options.C: may absorb the same energy if heat capacities are equal; conduction describes rate/path, not stored Q

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: C. 2021 misconception: conductor ≠ larger heat capacity. Conduction ≠ capacity.

Heat & Gases.question: In the equation pV = nRT, n stands for

options.B: number of moles

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. n is the number of moles. Number of molecules is N = nNA — do not swap them.

Heat & Gases.question: Which statement about latent heat is correct?

options.A: During melting at the melting point, temperature rises steadily as latent heat is absorbed
options.B: Latent heat of vaporization is energy per unit mass to change liquid↔vapour at constant T
options.C: Latent heat only applies to water
options.D: Latent heat equals mcΔT for any process

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Latent heat of vaporization is energy per unit mass for liquid↔vapour at constant T. During melting/boiling, temperature does not rise (that would be sensible heat mcΔT).

Heat & Gases.question: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on

options.B: volume alone
options.D: how the gas was compressed historically

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: C. State function for ideal gas U(T). Path myths common.

Heat & Gases.question: In a vacuum flask, the vacuum between walls mainly reduces heat transfer by

options.B: conduction and convection

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Vacuum removes the medium for conduction and convection; silvered walls mainly cut radiation.

Heat & Gases.question: Absolute zero on the kelvin scale is the temperature at which

options.B: an ideal gas would have zero volume/pressure extrapolating from Charles’s law behaviour
options.C: all real molecular motion in every material has been proven to stop completely for all substances
options.D: Celsius and kelvin readings are equal

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Absolute zero is defined via ideal-gas / thermodynamic extrapolation (zero volume or pressure on Charles’s law). Real molecular motion does not literally stop in every material.

Heat & Gases.question: Heat capacity C of an object is

options.A: energy to raise temperature by 1 K (for that object)
options.B: energy per kg per K
options.D: always equal to mc with c of water

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: A. Heat capacity C is energy to raise that object’s temperature by 1 K; specific heat capacity c is per unit mass. Neither equals thermal conductivity.

Heat & Gases.question: On a sunny day a dark car roof feels hotter than a light roof mainly because the dark surface

options.B: absorbs more thermal radiation

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. Kirchhoff/radiation fact; D false (good absorbers are good emitters).

Heat & Gases.question: When compressed gas is pumped into a structure at the seabed, its pressure must be

options.B: greater than the surrounding water pressure at that depth
options.C: less than water pressure so water can push it in

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. To inflate against the surroundings, gas pressure must exceed the water pressure at that depth.

Heat & Gases.question: Relation between pressure, force and area is

options.B: p = F / A

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. By definition pressure p = F/A (force per unit area).

Heat & Gases.question: During boiling of pure water at constant pressure, adding heat mainly

options.B: increases average KE of liquid molecules without phase change
options.C: provides latent heat to convert liquid to vapour at constant T

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: C. At constant pressure boiling, heat supplies latent heat for liquid→vapour at constant temperature, not a rise in temperature.

Heat & Gases.question: Charles’s law (constant p) relates volume and temperature. Temperature must be measured from

options.B: an absolute (kelvin) scale for the linear V ∝ T form through origin
options.D: the ice point as zero with V ∝ t(°C) through origin

Heat & Gases.explanation: Correct answer: B. V ∝ T through the origin only if T is on an absolute (kelvin) scale; Celsius does not give that form.

Waves.question: Sound waves are transverse waves.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. Sound waves are longitudinal waves. The particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of energy propagation.

Waves.question: When you look at an object at the bottom of a pool, it appears to be deeper than it really is.
Waves.explanation: False. Due to refraction (light bending away from the normal as it leaves the water), the apparent depth is less than the real depth. The object appears shallower.

Waves.question: A short-sighted (myopic) person cannot see nearby objects clearly, and their condition is corrected using a convex lens.
Waves.explanation: False. A short-sighted person cannot see distant objects clearly (their far point is too close). The condition is corrected using a concave (diverging) lens.

Waves.question: The speed of a wave (v) is determined by the properties of the medium, so changing the source's frequency (f) will not change the wave's speed.
Waves.explanation: Correct. While v = fλ is true, the speed (v) is constant for a given medium. If you change the frequency (f) of the source, the wavelength (λ) will adjust accordingly (λ = v/f), but v remains the same.

Waves.question: In a diffraction grating, red light is diffracted at a larger angle than violet light for the same order of maximum.
Waves.explanation: Correct. According to the grating equation d sin(θ) = nλ, the angle of diffraction (θ) is directly proportional to the wavelength (λ). Since red light has a longer wavelength than violet light, it diffracts more.

Waves.question: The amplitude of a wave is related to its energy.
Waves.explanation: Correct. The energy carried by a wave is proportional to the square of its amplitude. A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy.

Waves.question: When light passes from air into water, its frequency changes.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. When a wave passes from one medium to another, its frequency remains constant because it is determined by the source. Its speed and wavelength change, but the frequency does not.

Waves.question: Constructive interference occurs when a crest meets a trough.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. Constructive interference occurs when two crests or two troughs meet, resulting in a wave of larger amplitude. When a crest meets a trough, destructive interference occurs.

Waves.question: A stationary wave transmits energy from one point to another.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. A stationary (or standing) wave does not transfer energy. Energy is localized in segments between the nodes. Progressive (traveling) waves transfer energy.

Waves.question: The refractive index of a medium can be less than 1.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. The refractive index (n) is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum (c) to the speed of light in the medium (v), so n = c/v. Since light travels fastest in a vacuum, v is always less than or equal to c, meaning n is always greater than or equal to 1.

Waves.question: Sound travels faster in air than in steel.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. Sound travels much faster in solids like steel than in gases like air. This is because the particles in a solid are much closer together and more rigidly connected, allowing vibrations to be transmitted more efficiently.

Waves.question: The pitch of a sound is determined by its amplitude.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. The pitch of a sound is determined by its frequency. The amplitude of a sound wave determines its loudness or intensity.

Waves.question: When a wave is reflected from a fixed end, it is inverted.
Waves.explanation: Correct. When a wave on a string reflects from a fixed end, it undergoes a 180° phase change, meaning it is inverted. If it reflects from a free end, there is no phase change.

Waves.question: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels from a denser medium to a less dense medium.
Waves.explanation: Correct. Total internal reflection happens when light travels from a medium with a higher refractive index to one with a lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.

Waves.question: Ultrasound is a sound wave with a very high amplitude.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. Ultrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies above the range of human hearing (typically > 20,000 Hz). Its amplitude is not necessarily high.

Waves.question: Electromagnetic waves require a medium to travel.
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. Electromagnetic waves, such as light and radio waves, are disturbances in electric and magnetic fields and can travel through a vacuum. Mechanical waves (like sound) require a medium.

Waves.question: The loudness of a sound is measured in Hertz (Hz).
Waves.explanation: Incorrect. The loudness or sound intensity level is measured in decibels (dB). Frequency is measured in Hertz (Hz).

Waves.question: For a stationary wave on a string, any point at a node has zero displacement at all times.
Waves.explanation: True. This is the definition of a node.

Waves.question: For a stationary wave, a point at an antinode vibrates sinusoidally with maximum amplitude A.
Waves.explanation: True. This is the definition of an antinode.

Waves.question: A single snapshot of a stationary wave uniquely reveals the period.
Waves.explanation: False. A snapshot gives the spatial pattern, not the temporal period.

Waves.question: In a glass prism, violet light deviates more than red because its refractive index is higher (violet travels slower).
Waves.explanation: True. This is due to normal dispersion in glass.

Waves.question: A typical ultraviolet wavelength in vacuum is of order 10⁻⁷ m.
Waves.explanation: True. The UV range is approximately 10–400 nm.

Waves.question: A typical microwave wavelength in vacuum is of order 10⁻⁵ m.
Waves.explanation: False. Microwaves are typically in the range of ~10⁻² to 10⁻¹ m.

Waves.question: On a given string, doubling the driving frequency doubles the wave speed.
Waves.explanation: False. The wave speed v ≈ √(T/μ) is set by the string's tension and mass per unit length, not by the driving frequency.

Waves.question: On the same string, changing the frequency changes the wavelength but not (to first order) the wave speed.
Waves.explanation: True. This follows from the wave equation v = fλ.

Waves.question: When a standing wave pattern shifts from one harmonic to the next, some pairs of points that were out of phase can become in phase.
Waves.explanation: True. The mode shapes change the phase relations between points.

Waves.question: In a stretched string, nodes are at fixed ends; the second harmonic has twice as many loops as the first.
Waves.explanation: True. This describes the relationship between mode numbers.

Waves.question: In a longitudinal wave, equilibrium positions are fixed; particles oscillate about them.
Waves.explanation: True. Medium particles vibrate around fixed equilibrium positions.

Waves.question: A particle is momentarily at rest whenever it passes through the equilibrium position.
Waves.explanation: False. It moves fastest at the equilibrium position.

Waves.question: Two waves of different frequencies cannot be superposed at the same point.
Waves.explanation: False. The superposition principle still applies; the resultant wave varies in time (beats are possible).

Waves.question: Submarines use ultrasound instead of microwaves mainly because microwaves are strongly absorbed by seawater.
Waves.explanation: True. Water is lossy at microwave frequencies.

Waves.question: When two pulses on a string meet, the instantaneous shape is the algebraic sum of their displacements.
Waves.explanation: True. This is the superposition principle for waves on strings.

Waves.question: In a standing wave on a string, the distance between adjacent nodes equals half a wavelength.
Waves.explanation: True. The spacing between a node and an antinode is λ/4, so the node-to-node distance is λ/2.

Waves.question: In a standing wave, all points within the same loop (between two adjacent nodes) oscillate in phase; neighboring loops are in antiphase.
Waves.explanation: True. This is the standard phase relationship for standing waves.

Waves.question: In a longitudinal wave, particle displacement is parallel to the direction of wave propagation.
Waves.explanation: True. This is the definition of a longitudinal wave.

Waves.question: In simple harmonic oscillation of a particle in a wave, the particle’s speed is maximum at its equilibrium position.
Waves.explanation: True. Maximum velocity occurs at zero displacement in SHM.

Waves.question: With white light on a diffraction grating, the central maximum appears white because all wavelengths overlap at θ = 0.
Waves.explanation: True. The m = 0 order is achromatic, meaning it is not spread into colors.

Waves.question: Higher diffraction orders in a grating spread colors more than lower orders.
Waves.explanation: True. From θ ≈ arcsin(mλ/d), a larger order 'm' increases the angular spread by wavelength.

Waves.question: Two incoherent sources will not produce a stable, observable interference pattern even though waves still superpose physically.
Waves.explanation: True. Random phase differences destroy the conditions for stationary fringes.

Waves.question: For coherent sources, increasing the source separation decreases fringe spacing (closer fringes).
Waves.explanation: True. Fringe spacing is inversely proportional to the separation of the sources.

Waves.question: Antinodal lines from two coherent point sources on water are curved, not straight.
Waves.explanation: True. The loci of points with a constant path difference form hyperbolas, which are curved.

Waves.question: A mirage requires a refractive-index gradient near hot ground that bends rays by refraction.
Waves.explanation: True. Thermal gradients in the air create a non-uniform refractive index that curves light paths.

Waves.question: At an interface from a higher to a lower refractive index (e.g., plastic to air), a refracted ray bends away from the normal.
Waves.explanation: True. This is a direct consequence of Snell’s law.

Waves.question: A ray totally internally reflecting within a block may later emerge if at a subsequent boundary its incidence angle becomes smaller than the critical angle.
Waves.explanation: True. The internal geometry of the block can change the incidence angle at the next surface.

Waves.question: Peak-to-trough displacement of a sinusoidal wave equals 2A if the amplitude is A.
Waves.explanation: True. This is by definition of amplitude, which is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium position.

Waves.question: In echo sounding, the travel time corresponds to a one-way trip to the seabed.
Waves.explanation: False. The time measured is for a round trip (down and back).

Waves.question: When a water wave travels from shallow to deep water, its frequency

options.B: decreases

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: C. Frequency is set by the source and stays the same; speed and wavelength change with depth.

Waves.question: When light enters glass from air, its frequency

options.B: decreases

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: C. Frequency is unchanged at the boundary; in glass the speed drops and so wavelength drops (v = fλ).

Waves.question: On a stretched string, if frequency doubles while tension and mass/length fixed, wave speed

options.B: halves

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: C. On a given string, wave speed depends on tension and μ, not on driving frequency; doubling f halves λ.

Waves.question: In a longitudinal sound wave, a particle at the equilibrium position

options.B: may have maximum speed there (like SHM through centre)
options.C: only moves perpendicular to wave travel

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Like SHM through the centre, a particle at the equilibrium position can have maximum speed (zero displacement, max |v|).

Waves.question: Particle motion in a longitudinal wave is

options.B: parallel to propagation

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. In a longitudinal wave, particle oscillation is parallel to the direction of propagation.

Waves.question: Two waves of different frequencies at one point

options.A: always reinforce to a larger fixed amplitude
options.B: do not form a steady interference maximum like equal-f coherent sources

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Steady interference maxima need equal frequencies and coherence; different frequencies do not lock a fixed fringe pattern.

Waves.question: Stable interference fringes from two sources require the sources to be

options.B: coherent (constant phase relation)

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Stable fringes need coherent sources (constant phase difference). ‘Out of phase’ is not the same as incoherent.

Waves.question: Microwaves in air travel at approximately

options.B: speed of light

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Microwaves are electromagnetic waves, so in air they travel at nearly the speed of light.

Waves.question: An echo sounding measures depth using travel time t. Distance is proportional to

options.B: ½ vt (there and back)

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. The pulse travels to the reflector and back, so depth = ½ vt, not vt.

Waves.question: Apparent depth of a pool floor viewed from air is

options.B: shallower than real

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Refraction makes the pool floor look shallower than its real depth when viewed from air.

Waves.question: A short-sighted (myopic) person cannot see distant objects clearly. Correction uses a

options.B: concave (diverging) lens

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Myopia focuses distant rays in front of the retina; a diverging (concave) lens corrects it.

Waves.question: A ray in denser medium meets a boundary with air. If it refracts into air, it bends

options.B: away from the normal

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Entering a less dense medium (denser→air), the ray speeds up and bends away from the normal.

Waves.question: Diffraction and refraction are

options.A: the same effect with different names
options.B: different: refraction = speed/direction change across media; diffraction = spreading at obstacles/apertures

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Refraction is change of speed/direction across media; diffraction is spreading at obstacles or apertures — different effects.

Waves.question: EM spectrum: which travels at c in vacuum?

options.B: only radio

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: C. All electromagnetic waves travel at c in vacuum, from radio through γ rays.

Waves.question: Constructive interference of two coherent waves of equal amplitude occurs when path difference is

options.B: nλ
options.C: always zero only if amplitudes differ

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. For coherent equal-amplitude waves, constructive interference occurs when path difference is an integer number of wavelengths (nλ).

Waves.question: For ultrasound imaging of fine detail, higher frequency generally gives

options.A: worse resolution but is chosen because ‘less harmful’
options.B: better resolution (shorter λ), with penetration trade-offs

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Higher frequency means shorter wavelength, which improves resolution; penetration into tissue usually falls.

Waves.question: Polarisation is a property that demonstrates

options.B: light (EM) has transverse character

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Polarisation shows transverse character; longitudinal sound waves in air cannot be polarised that way.

Waves.question: In Young’s double slit, increasing slit separation a (other things fixed) makes fringe spacing

options.B: smaller

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. Fringe spacing Δy = λD/a, so larger slit separation a gives closer fringes.

Waves.question: Amplitude of a mechanical wave is most directly related to

options.B: energy/intensity carried
options.C: wave speed in the medium only

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: B. For a mechanical wave, amplitude is most directly linked to the energy (and intensity) it carries.

Waves.question: Critical angle for glass→air depends on

options.A: only the refractive index of glass relative to air (and geometry definition)
options.B: the colour of the observer’s shirt

Waves.explanation: Correct answer: A. Critical angle for glass→air depends on the refractive indices (sin c = 1/n for glass to air), not on colour of clothing, B-field, or glass thickness alone.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The resistance of a metallic conductor typically decreases as its temperature increases.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. For a metallic conductor, resistance increases with temperature. Higher temperature causes the metal ions to vibrate more, leading to more frequent collisions with the charge carriers (electrons) and thus impeding their flow.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A transformer can step up DC voltage.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. Transformers operate on the principle of mutual electromagnetic induction, which requires a changing magnetic flux. DC current produces a constant magnetic field, so it cannot induce a current in the secondary coil. Transformers only work with AC.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: According to Lenz's law, the induced current will flow in a direction that opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. This is the fundamental statement of Lenz's law. It's a consequence of the conservation of energy, ensuring that you have to do work to create the induced current.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a uniform electric field, the electric potential increases in the direction of the electric field lines.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. Electric field lines point from regions of higher potential to regions of lower potential. Therefore, electric potential decreases in the direction of the electric field.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Adding resistors in parallel decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. When resistors are added in parallel, more paths are available for the current to flow, which reduces the overall resistance. The equivalent resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The magnetic field inside a long solenoid is strongest at its ends.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. The magnetic field inside a long, ideal solenoid is nearly uniform and strongest in its center, far from the ends. The field becomes weaker and diverges outside the ends.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: An electron moving parallel to a magnetic field line will experience a magnetic force.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. The magnetic force on a charged particle is given by F = qvBsin(θ). If the velocity (v) is parallel to the magnetic field (B), the angle θ is 0°, and sin(0°) = 0, so the force is zero.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Ohm's law (V=IR) is a fundamental law of physics and is always obeyed by all materials.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. Ohm's law is an empirical relationship that holds true for many materials (ohmic materials) under certain conditions. It is not a fundamental law, and many devices (like diodes and transistors) are non-ohmic.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A capacitor stores energy in its magnetic field.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. A capacitor stores energy in the electric field between its plates. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The Earth's magnetic north pole is located at the geographic North Pole.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. The Earth's magnetic north pole (where a compass needle points) is actually a magnetic south pole, located near the geographic North Pole. Opposite poles attract.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Kirchhoff's junction rule is a consequence of the conservation of charge.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. The junction rule states that the total current entering a junction must equal the total current leaving it. This is a direct statement that charge does not accumulate at a junction.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a step-up transformer, the current in the secondary coil is greater than the current in the primary coil.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. For an ideal transformer, power is conserved (P_in = P_out, so V_p * I_p = V_s * I_s). If the voltage is stepped up (V_s > V_p), the current must be stepped down (I_s < I_p) to conserve power.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electric field lines can cross each other.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. Electric field lines can never cross. If they did, it would imply that the electric field has two different directions at the same point, which is impossible.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A voltmeter should have a very high internal resistance.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component it measures. To avoid drawing significant current from the circuit and altering the voltage it is intended to measure, it must have a very high resistance.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The force between two parallel current-carrying wires is attractive if the currents are in opposite directions.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. The force is attractive if the currents are in the same direction and repulsive if they are in opposite directions.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: An ammeter should be connected in series and have a very high resistance.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. An ammeter is connected in series to measure the current flowing through a part of the circuit. It must have a very low resistance so that it does not significantly impede the current it is trying to measure.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The unit of capacitance, the Farad, is equivalent to a Coulomb per Volt.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. Capacitance is defined as the ratio of charge stored to the potential difference (C = Q/V), so its unit, the Farad (F), is equivalent to C/V.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A moving electric charge produces both an electric and a magnetic field.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct. A stationary charge produces only an electric field. A moving charge (a current) produces both an electric field and a magnetic field.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: For charges −4Q and +Q on a line, the point where the net electric field is zero lies outside the segment between them.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. Between them, the fields point in the same direction; cancellation occurs outside, near the side of the smaller-magnitude charge.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In electromagnetic induction, the induced magnetic torque on a rotating coil opposes its rotation.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is a direct consequence of Lenz’s law.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The induced e.m.f. in a rotating coil is maximum when the plane of the coil is parallel to the field.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The rate of change of magnetic flux, |dΦ/dt|, is maximum at this orientation (θ = 90°).

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The r.m.s. voltage of a sinusoid is Vp/√2; changing frequency does not change Vrms if Vp is fixed.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is the definition of Vrms for a sinusoidal voltage.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a simple d.c. motor with a split-ring commutator, the current reverses every half-turn.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is necessary to maintain continuous rotation.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: For a rod moving across rails in a uniform B into the page, the induced emf magnitude is Bdv, where d is the rail separation.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The induced EMF is ℰ = Blv, with l being the separation of the rails (the active length).

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Transformers: Total output power equals (number of bulbs) × (rated power per bulb); input power equals output/efficiency.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. P_out = ΣP_rated, and P_in = P_out/η.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electric field vectors add by vector addition; the resultant at a point is the vector sum of contributions from all charges.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is the principle of superposition.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The electrical resistance between opposite faces of a metallic cube of side x is proportional to 1/x.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. R = ρL/A = ρx/x² = ρ/x.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A metal rod moving across a magnetic field with open terminals has an induced emf but no induced current; hence no magnetic drag force acts on it.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. With no circuit, there is no current, so there is no force F = IL×B.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Resistivity is a property of an object, while resistance is a property of a material.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Incorrect. It is the other way around. Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic property of a material. Resistance (R) is a property of a specific object that depends on its material (resistivity), length, and cross-sectional area (R = ρL/A).

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electric shock severity depends primarily on current through the body, not voltage alone.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. A high voltage is dangerous mainly because it can drive a large and harmful current through you.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A bird perched on a single high-voltage line is usually safe because the potential difference across its feet is tiny, so negligible current flows through its body.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The bird is at a nearly uniform high potential, so there is no significant voltage drop across its body.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Resistance depends on cross-sectional area, not surface area.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The formula is R = ρL/A, where A is the perpendicular cross-sectional area.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a search-coil experiment inside a solenoid, the induced emf is maximized when the coil’s plane is perpendicular to the field lines (coil axis parallel to B).
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This orientation maximizes the change in flux linkage as the coil is moved or the field is changed.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Bulbs connected in parallel share the same potential difference; hence energy dissipated per unit charge is the same for each bulb.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is the definition of potential difference (voltage).

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In that parallel-bulb circuit, the brighter bulb dissipates more power per second and carries a larger current.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. Since P = VI and V is the same for both, a larger power P implies a larger current I.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a moving rod within a magnetic field, the end indicated by v × B (for positive charges) becomes the positive terminal of the induced emf.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This describes the direction of charge separation due to the magnetic force.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: If the moving-rod circuit is closed, the induced current generates a magnetic force opposing the motion.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is a direct consequence of Lenz’s law, where the force F opposes the velocity v.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The magnetic force on a straight current-carrying wire is maximal when the wire is perpendicular to B and zero when parallel to B.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The force is given by F = B I L sinθ.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a rectangular coil, segments parallel to the magnetic field experience negligible magnetic force; torque comes mainly from the sides perpendicular to B.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is due to the sinθ dependence of the magnetic force.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a current-carrying spring, adjacent wire segments with currents in the same direction attract each other; in opposite directions they repel.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is the basis of magnetic deformation in springs and coils.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Two parallel long conductors carrying currents in the same direction attract each other.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is a standard result of Ampere’s force law.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a uniform electric field, charged particles follow parabolic trajectories (constant acceleration a = qE/m), neglecting other forces.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is analogous to projectile motion under gravity.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In the same electric field, α-particles deflect much less than β-particles because of the α’s much larger mass and lower charge-to-mass ratio.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. Since a = qE/m and the mass of an alpha particle is much greater than an electron, its acceleration is much smaller.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: When summing electric fields from multiple point charges, vector addition (component-wise) must be used; magnitudes do not simply add.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This was a point of struggle for candidates involving vector sums.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: For two identical positive charges placed symmetrically, the electric field at the midpoint is non-zero and points outward along the symmetry axis.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. The fields from each charge add together, they do not cancel out.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: The instantaneous induced emf in a rotating coil is proportional to the time rate of change of flux, ℰ = −d(NΦ)/dt, not to the flux itself.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This explains why the emf is maximum when the flux is changing fastest.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: When the coil’s plane is perpendicular to B (flux maximum), the induced emf is instantaneously zero.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. At this point, the rate of change of flux, dΦ/dt, is zero.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In the rotating frame example, the magnetic braking torque is opposite to the rotation at all instants (Lenz’s law).
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. Induced effects always oppose the change that produces them.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A protective resistor placed in the ammeter branch limits current and helps prevent meter damage if misused.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This is the purpose of the protective resistor in the circuit.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In parallel networks, the potential difference across each branch equals the source potential difference.
Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: True. This fundamental circuit rule was missed by some.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A metal rod moves in a magnetic field but is not part of a closed circuit. There can be

options.A: an induced current along the rod anyway
options.B: an induced e.m.f. (charge separation) but no sustained current
options.C: neither e.m.f. nor any charge shift

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Motional e.m.f. can separate charges on an open rod, but a sustained current needs a closed circuit.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Magnetic force on a current-carrying wire is

options.B: perpendicular to B (and to I) when F = BIL sinθ

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Magnetic force on a current is perpendicular to both B and I (F = BIL sinθ), not parallel to B.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Open conducting rod moving in B: opposing magnetic drag force

options.B: requires induced current; without closed path, no magnetic drag of that kind
options.D: is electrostatic only and always huge

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Magnetic drag from induction needs an induced current; with no closed path there is no such magnetic drag.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: When magnetic flux through a rotating coil is instantaneously zero, induced e.m.f./current is

options.B: often maximum because dΦ/dt is largest then

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Induced e.m.f. depends on dΦ/dt, not on Φ itself — when flux is zero mid-swing, the rate of change is often largest.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Eddy-current braking on a vehicle

options.A: works even when the vehicle is completely at rest
options.B: needs relative motion / changing flux while moving

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Eddy-current braking needs relative motion (changing flux); it does not act when the vehicle is fully at rest.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: After the field of a coil becomes steady, eddy currents in a nearby metal ring

options.B: stop (no changing flux) so magnetic lift/force from eddy effects ceases

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Eddy currents need changing flux; once the field is steady they stop and the related magnetic force ceases.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Unlike magnetic poles

options.B: attract

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Unlike magnetic poles attract. Magnetic poles are not the same as ± electric charges.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Raising resistance of a heater on fixed mains voltage

options.A: increases power (P = V²/R falls when R rises)
options.B: decreases power for fixed V

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. For fixed V, P = V²/R, so raising resistance lowers power — a common trap is thinking power rises.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Mains ‘220 V’ in HK normally means

options.B: r.m.s. voltage

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Mains ‘220 V’ in Hong Kong means the r.m.s. voltage, not the peak.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electric shock hazard is primarily due to

options.A: high voltage by itself with zero current
options.B: large current through the body
options.D: colour of the wire insulation only

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Shock hazard comes from a large current through the body; voltage alone with no current path is not the injury mechanism.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: A bird can perch on a single high-voltage bare cable mainly because

options.A: the cable is always thickly insulated
options.B: both feet are at nearly the same potential so little current through the bird
options.D: voltage is zero on all cables

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Both feet are at nearly the same potential on one wire, so little current flows through the bird — not because the cable is insulated.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In a simple d.c. motor, current in the armature coil

options.A: keeps one direction all the time without commutation
options.B: is reversed each half-turn by the commutator so torque direction stays useful

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. The commutator reverses armature current each half-turn so the torque keeps driving rotation in one sense.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Charged particle moving in uniform B (F magnetic only)

options.B: speed stays the same; direction can change (circular/helical)

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Magnetic force is always ⊥ to v, so it changes direction but not speed; KE stays constant (circular/helical path).

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electron moving parallel to B experiences magnetic force

options.B: zero (sinθ = 0)

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. F = qvB sinθ; if v is parallel to B then sinθ = 0, so magnetic force is zero.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Lamps dark in a circuit may be

options.B: open OR shorted (bypassed) — need to diagnose

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. A dark lamp can be open-circuit or shorted/bypassed — you must diagnose which, not assume only open.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Adding identical resistors in parallel

options.B: decreases total resistance

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Parallel paths add conductance, so total resistance falls when identical resistors are added in parallel.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Transformer action requires

options.B: changing flux (usually a.c.) linking coils

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. A transformer needs changing flux linking the coils (usually a.c.); steady d.c. does not induce a secondary e.m.f.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Electric field direction is the direction of force on a

options.B: positive test charge

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. By definition, E-field direction is the force on a positive test charge; potential decreases along field lines.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Resistance R of a uniform wire satisfies

options.B: R ∝ ℓ / A

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. R = ρℓ/A, so resistance rises with length and falls with cross-sectional area.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: In parallel branches, energy transferred per unit charge through each branch (from same two nodes) is

options.A: larger in the brighter lamp only because brightness means higher V
options.B: the same (same pd); brightness differences come from current/power

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Parallel branches share the same pd, so energy per unit charge (V) is the same; brightness differs via current and power.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Lenz’s law: induced current direction

options.B: opposes the change in flux that produces it
options.D: is always from N to S outside magnets only

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Lenz’s law: the induced current’s direction opposes the change in flux that produces it.

Electricity & Magnetism.question: Magnetic field along the axis inside a long solenoid is

options.A: strongest at the ends and zero in middle
options.B: approximately uniform and strong inside, weaker outside

Electricity & Magnetism.explanation: Correct answer: B. Inside a long solenoid the field is approximately uniform and strong; it is weaker outside — not strongest only at the ends.

Radiation.question: Nuclear fusion is

options.A: always a spontaneous process like α decay
options.B: not generally spontaneous; needs extreme conditions to overcome repulsion
options.C: the splitting of a heavy nucleus

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Fusion of light nuclei is not generally spontaneous; nuclei must overcome electrostatic repulsion under extreme conditions (unlike α decay).

Radiation.question: A film badge worn in air is generally unsuitable for monitoring α exposure because

options.B: α have very short range in air and usually don’t reach the badge
options.C: α are undetectable by any film

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. α particles have a very short range in air, so they usually never reach a film badge worn in air — not because they are too penetrating.

Radiation.question: Isotopes of an element have

options.A: same mass number, different atomic number
options.B: same atomic number Z, different mass number A (different N)
options.D: different Z and different chemical behaviour always as different elements

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Isotopes share the same atomic number Z (same element) but different mass number A (different neutron number).

Radiation.question: Binding energy of a nucleus is

options.A: energy you must supply to assemble nucleons into the nucleus
options.B: energy required to separate the nucleus into individual nucleons
options.C: always equal to mc² of one electron
options.D: the kinetic energy of α particles only

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Binding energy is the energy needed to separate a nucleus into free nucleons (or released when they assemble).

Radiation.question: Moderator in a thermal fission reactor slows

options.B: neutrons
options.C: α particles in fuel rods as primary purpose

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. The moderator slows fast neutrons so they are more likely to cause fission in a thermal reactor — not electrons or α particles.

Radiation.question: Most α particles pass straight through thin gold foil. This observation alone

options.A: is enough to rule out Thomson’s plum-pudding model
options.B: fits both plum-pudding and nuclear models, so does not by itself invalidate Thomson

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Straight-through α tracks fit both plum-pudding and nuclear models; large-angle scatters are what rule out Thomson.

Radiation.question: γ radiation in a magnetic field is

options.B: undeflected (uncharged EM radiation)

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. γ rays are uncharged electromagnetic radiation, so a magnetic field does not deflect them.

Radiation.question: A pure radioisotope that appears to emit α, β and γ may do so because

options.A: the sample must be chemically impure
options.B: a decay series / daughter products contribute different radiations

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. A decay chain’s parent and daughters can emit different radiations, so a ‘pure’ starting nuclide may appear to give α, β and γ together.

Radiation.question: Very long half-life means
