options.A: activity is automatically negligible and always harmless regardless of quantity
options.B: decay is slow per nucleus; hazard still depends on amount, type, and exposure

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Long half-life means slow decay per nucleus; total hazard still depends on amount, radiation type and exposure — it is not automatically harmless.

Radiation.question: Nuclear fission is

options.B: splitting a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Fission is splitting a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei; fusion is combining light nuclei.

Radiation.question: α particles ‘neutralise’ charged smoke/dust in a detector mainly by

options.A: chemically combining with dust particles directly as the whole story
options.B: ionising air; ions then neutralise charged particles

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. α particles ionise air; the ions then neutralise charged smoke/dust — not by chemically sticking to dust as the whole story.

Radiation.question: Half-life is the time for

options.B: half the nuclei (of a large sample) to decay

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Half-life is the time for half the nuclei in a large sample to decay — not for all to decay or for activity to reach zero.

Radiation.question: Power delivered by a radioisotope heat source depends most directly on

options.A: total number of atoms ignoring decay rate
options.B: activity (decays per second) and energy per decay

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Thermal power scales with decays per second (activity) and energy released per decay.

Radiation.question: If moderator water is lost in a thermal reactor, the chain reaction may stop because

options.B: supply of slowed neutrons for fission is lost
options.C: neutrons become too slow to do anything ever

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Without moderator water, neutrons are not slowed for thermal fission, so the chain reaction can stop.

Radiation.question: α, β, γ ionising ability / penetrating power (qualitative)

options.B: α least penetrating (stopped by paper/few cm air); γ most penetrating of the three

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. α ionise strongly but penetrate least (paper / few cm air); γ penetrate most of the three.

Radiation.question: Energy invested in pushing two nuclei together against electrostatic repulsion is stored mainly as

options.A: random heat only with no potential
options.B: electrical potential energy
options.C: nuclear binding already more negative automatically

Radiation.explanation: Correct answer: B. Work done against electrostatic repulsion is stored as electrical potential energy of the two nuclei.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: The kilowatt-hour (kW·h) is a unit of

options.B: energy

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: B. Power is in W or kW; energy = power × time, so the kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: A domestic appliance rated 2 kW runs for 3 hours. Energy transferred from the mains is closest to

options.B: 6 kW

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: A. E = Pt = 2 kW × 3 h = 6 kW·h. A confuses energy with power.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Electricity tariff charges are usually based mainly on

options.B: resistance of wiring only

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: C. Domestic cost tracks energy consumed (and sometimes demand), not voltage or frequency alone.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Regenerative braking on a vehicle mainly recovers energy by

options.A: converting kinetic energy of the vehicle into electrical energy to recharge a battery
options.B: storing heat from friction pads as electrical energy
options.D: turning gravitational PE of the road into chemical energy in petrol

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: A. Regenerative braking converts the vehicle’s kinetic energy into electrical energy stored in a battery — not friction heat into electricity.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: If a regenerative-braking battery is already full, the vehicle

options.B: must accelerate until the battery empties
options.D: can still be stopped using ordinary friction brakes (regen may be limited)

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: D. Ordinary friction brakes still work if the regen battery is full; battery state does not remove mechanical braking.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: On a level road at steady speed against constant drag, a heavier vehicle compared with a lighter one

options.A: always needs much larger driving force just to keep that same steady speed
options.B: needs zero power
options.C: does not need extra driving force merely because of mass; extra force/power matters mainly when accelerating

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: C. At steady speed, drive force balances drag; extra mass matters mainly when accelerating, not just to hold the same speed against the same drag.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Power and work done are

options.A: different: power is the rate of doing work / transferring energy
options.B: the same physical quantity

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: A. Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy (P = W/t or P = Fv); work and power are not the same quantity.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Lamp luminous efficacy and electrical efficiency are

options.A: always identical names for the same ratio
options.B: both measured only in ohms
options.D: related ideas but not the same: efficacy concerns useful light per electrical power; efficiency is broader energy conversion

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: D. Luminous efficacy is useful light output per electrical power; electrical efficiency is a broader energy-conversion ratio — related ideas, not identical.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Painting a photovoltaic solar cell’s active surface black

options.A: must raise electrical energy output because black absorbs more radiation
options.B: makes efficiency automatically 100%
options.C: need not raise electrical output: absorption as heat is not the same as photovoltaic conversion
options.D: turns sunlight into chemical energy in silicon always

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: C. Black surfaces absorb more radiation as heat, but that does not automatically raise photovoltaic electrical output.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: In a simple solar–battery setup, useful bookkeeping of energy forms should include that

options.A: solar input is electromagnetic radiation; the battery stores chemical energy when charged
options.B: the Sun’s thermal energy is converted directly to electricity and the battery’s chemical store can be ignored

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: A. Solar input is EM radiation; a charged battery stores chemical energy. Do not skip the chemical store or call the chain merely ‘thermal→electrical’.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: A building material with a larger U-value (other things equal) means

options.A: better insulation (less heat loss rate per area per temperature difference)
options.B: higher electrical resistivity
options.D: poorer insulation: higher thermal transmittance / faster heat loss for given ΔT and area

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: D. U-value = heat transfer rate per unit area per unit temperature difference — higher U ⇒ worse insulator (Energy: building performance).

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Double glazing reduces heat loss through a window mainly by

options.B: trapping a poorly conducting gas/air layer so conduction/convection across the pane gap falls

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: B. Insulation qualitative: trapped air / gap cuts conduction–convection (Energy: buildings).

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Which is a renewable energy source in the usual DSE classification sense?

options.B: natural gas

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: C. Wind is classed as renewable; coal, natural gas and petroleum are non-renewable fossil fuels.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Fossil fuels are classed as non-renewable mainly because

options.A: they release no energy when burned
options.B: they form far more slowly than we use them
options.D: they have infinite reserves on human timescales

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: B. Fossil fuels form far more slowly than we consume them, so they are non-renewable on human timescales.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: For the same useful output, a process with higher efficiency

options.A: wastes a smaller fraction of input energy
options.B: wastes a larger fraction of input energy
options.D: has efficiency above 100% in a heat engine

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: A. η = useful output / input; higher η ⇒ less waste fraction.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: In a pressurised-water reactor (PWR), the pressurised primary coolant water typically

options.A: boils and that steam directly drives the turbine
options.B: is only a moderator and carries no heat
options.C: stays liquid under high pressure; heat is transferred to a secondary loop that produces steam for the turbine

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: C. In a PWR the pressurised primary coolant stays liquid; heat goes to a secondary loop that makes steam for the turbine.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Using LED lighting instead of an inefficient lamp for the same useful light generally

options.A: increases electrical energy use for that lighting task
options.B: changes the mains frequency
options.C: removes the need for any power source
options.D: reduces electrical energy use because more of the input becomes useful light (less waste heat per lumen)

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: D. Lighting / saving energy: higher efficacy → less electrical energy for same light.

Energy and Use of Energy.question: Transport energy efficiency discussions often emphasise that regenerative braking

options.A: replaces the need for any friction brakes forever
options.B: can return some kinetic energy to stored electrical energy, improving overall energy use on stop–go journeys
options.C: increases fuel use at every stop
options.D: only works on vehicles with empty fuel tanks

Energy and Use of Energy.explanation: Correct answer: B. Regenerative braking can return some kinetic energy to the battery, improving energy use on stop–go journeys — it does not replace friction brakes forever.

Atomic World.question: Alpha particles are positively charged.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, consisting of two protons and two neutrons, giving it a charge of +2e.

Atomic World.question: Gamma rays can be deflected by a magnetic field.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation (photons). They have no charge and therefore are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

Atomic World.question: Isotopes of an element have the same number of neutrons but a different number of protons.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons (which defines the element) but a different number of neutrons, resulting in a different mass number.

Atomic World.question: During beta decay, a neutron in the nucleus is converted into a proton and an electron.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. In beta-minus decay, a neutron transforms into a proton (which remains in the nucleus), and an electron (the beta particle) and an antineutrino are emitted.

Atomic World.question: Nuclear fission is the process of combining light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Nuclear fission is the process of splitting a heavy, unstable nucleus into two or more lighter nuclei. Combining light nuclei is called nuclear fusion.

Atomic World.question: The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes for half of its atoms to decay.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. This is the definition of half-life. After one half-life, the activity of the sample is also reduced by half.

Atomic World.question: In the Bohr model, electron angular momentum is quantized.
Atomic World.explanation: True. This is a foundational postulate of the Bohr model.

Atomic World.question: An electron dropping from n = 3 to n = 1 can produce three spectral lines in total.
Atomic World.explanation: True. The possible transitions are 3→1, 3→2, and 2→1.

Atomic World.question: Conventional film badges cannot reliably monitor alpha radiation exposure to workers.
Atomic World.explanation: True. Alpha particles are easily stopped by the badge’s covering and the air.

Atomic World.question: The stopping potential is equal to the maximum photoelectron kinetic energy divided by e.
Atomic World.explanation: True. The relationship is eVs = Kmax.

Atomic World.question: Increasing light frequency increases the saturation current.
Atomic World.explanation: False. The saturation current depends mainly on intensity; frequency changes Kmax.

Atomic World.question: In a uniform electric field, β-particles (electrons) are deflected more than α-particles, in opposite directions.
Atomic World.explanation: True. This is due to their much smaller mass and opposite charge.

Atomic World.question: Natural ionizing radiation can be found in sea water, rocks, and the human body.
Atomic World.explanation: True. These contain traces of radionuclides (e.g., K-40).

Atomic World.question: All of an atom's mass is concentrated in its nucleus.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. While the vast majority (over 99.9%) of an atom's mass is in the nucleus, the electrons orbiting the nucleus also contribute a small amount to the total mass.

Atomic World.question: The penetrating power of beta particles is generally greater than that of alpha particles.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. The order of penetrating power is typically gamma > beta > alpha. Alpha particles are large and highly ionizing, so they are stopped easily (by paper or skin). Beta particles are smaller and can penetrate further (stopped by thin aluminum).

Atomic World.question: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence principle is given by E = mc.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. The famous equation is E = mc², where 'c' is the speed of light. This relationship shows that mass and energy are interchangeable.

Atomic World.question: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of the incident light increases the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Increasing the intensity of the light increases the number of photons, which in turn increases the number of emitted electrons (the photoelectric current). The maximum kinetic energy of the electrons is determined by the frequency of the incident light, not its intensity.

Atomic World.question: A chain reaction in a nuclear reactor is controlled by using control rods that absorb protons.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Control rods, typically made of materials like boron or cadmium, control the reaction rate by absorbing excess neutrons, not protons.

Atomic World.question: Background radiation is solely due to man-made sources.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Background radiation comes from both natural sources (like radon gas, cosmic rays, radioactive elements in rocks) and man-made sources (like medical x-rays and nuclear fallout).

Atomic World.question: Nuclear fusion reactions release more energy per nucleon than fission reactions.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. While a single fission event releases more total energy than a single fusion event, fusion of light elements (like hydrogen) releases significantly more energy per unit of mass (per nucleon).

Atomic World.question: Rutherford's gold foil experiment proved the existence of the neutron.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. Rutherford's experiment led to the discovery of the atomic nucleus and the proposal of the planetary model of the atom. The neutron was discovered later by James Chadwick in 1932.

Atomic World.question: The strong nuclear force is responsible for holding electrons in orbit around the nucleus.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. The strong nuclear force is the force that binds protons and neutrons together within the nucleus. The electromagnetic force is responsible for keeping electrons in orbit.

Atomic World.question: Light exhibits properties of both a particle and a wave.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. This is the principle of wave-particle duality. Light can behave as an electromagnetic wave (showing diffraction and interference) and as a particle or photon (as seen in the photoelectric effect).

Atomic World.question: Radioactive decay is a random and spontaneous process.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. It is impossible to predict when a specific nucleus will decay. The process is governed by probability, which is why we use statistical measures like half-life to describe it for a large number of atoms.

Atomic World.question: The activity of a radioactive sample is measured in Joules.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. The activity of a radioactive sample (the rate of decay) is measured in Becquerels (Bq), where 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. Energy is measured in Joules.

Atomic World.question: An electron can exist in any orbit around a nucleus, as long as it has enough energy.
Atomic World.explanation: Incorrect. According to the Bohr model and quantum mechanics, electrons can only exist in specific, discrete energy levels or orbitals around the nucleus. They cannot exist in the spaces between these allowed orbits.

Atomic World.question: In a controlled nuclear fission reactor, the goal is to have the multiplication factor k exactly equal to 1.
Atomic World.explanation: Correct. A multiplication factor (k) of 1 means that each fission event causes, on average, exactly one other fission event. This leads to a self-sustaining chain reaction at a constant rate, which is known as a critical state.

Atomic World.question: In α-decay at rest, the α and daughter nucleus have equal and opposite momenta, but not equal kinetic energies.
Atomic World.explanation: True. They have the same momentum magnitude |p|, but KE ∝ p²/2m; the lighter α particle gets more KE.

Atomic World.question: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light (same frequency above threshold) mainly increases

options.A: the maximum kinetic energy of each photoelectron
options.B: the work function of the metal
options.C: the number of photoelectrons emitted per second (photocurrent), not Kmax
options.D: the threshold frequency of the metal

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: C. Higher intensity means more photons per second → more photoelectrons (larger photocurrent); Kmax depends on frequency, not intensity.

Atomic World.question: Increasing the frequency of incident light above threshold (intensity fixed) mainly

options.A: increases maximum photoelectron KE; saturation current is not set by frequency
options.B: increases saturation photocurrent in proportion to frequency

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. Higher frequency raises maximum photoelectron KE; saturation current is set by intensity (photon arrival rate), not frequency.

Atomic World.question: Stopping potential Vs in a photoelectric experiment satisfies

options.A: Vs equals Kmax numerically in joules with no conversion
options.B: eVs = Kmax
options.C: Vs equals the work function in eV always
options.D: Vs equals photon energy hf with no subtraction of work function

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: B. Stopping potential satisfies eVs = Kmax; Vs is not the work function, and it is not hf with no φ subtracted.

Atomic World.question: The work function of a metal is

options.A: equal to hf for any incident light used
options.B: the same as stopping potential in volts with no e factor
options.D: the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the surface; not simply “the photon energy” of whatever light is shining

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: D. Work function φ is the minimum energy to free an electron from the metal — not simply the photon energy hf of whatever light is shining.

Atomic World.question: Photoelectrons from a metal illuminated by monochromatic light show a spread of KE mainly because

options.A: electrons inside the metal need different energies to reach the surface (work function is a minimum); emission itself sets the spread
options.B: electrons lose random amounts of energy only while drifting from cathode to anode in the tube
options.C: the photon energy changes after each collision with air
options.D: magnetic fields in the lab quantise KE

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. Electrons need different energies to leave the surface (φ is a minimum), so emitted KE spreads; it is not mainly random losses on the flight to the anode.

Atomic World.question: The threshold frequency of a metal

options.A: rises whenever you use a higher-frequency lamp
options.B: is the same for all metals
options.C: is a property of the metal (linked to work function), not something that tracks the lamp frequency you happen to choose

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: C. Threshold frequency is a property of the metal (set by φ), not something that tracks the lamp frequency you choose.

Atomic World.question: In photoelectric equations, c in E = hc/λ is

options.B: the speed of light in vacuum (photon), not the electron’s speed

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: B. In E = hc/λ, c is the speed of light for the photon — not the photoelectron’s speed.

Atomic World.question: In the Bohr model of hydrogen, while the electron remains in an allowed orbit it

options.A: continuously radiates EM waves like a classical accelerating charge
options.B: must spiral into the nucleus in microseconds
options.D: does not radiate; energy of that stationary state stays constant until a jump

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: D. In Bohr’s model an electron in an allowed orbit does not radiate; energy stays fixed until a quantum jump.

Atomic World.question: A photon can excite a hydrogen atom from one Bohr level to a higher one only if

options.A: its energy matches the exact level difference ΔE (one photon ↔ one transition)
options.B: its energy is any value larger than the level gap ΔE
options.D: the photon energy equals the electron’s total energy at the upper level alone

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. One photon must match the exact level difference ΔE; photons do not pool half-energies, and photon energy is not the upper level’s En alone.

Atomic World.question: The first excited state of hydrogen corresponds to
Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: B. Ground state is n = 1; the first excited state is n = 2.

Atomic World.question: Bohr orbit radius scales as rn ∝ n². Compared with the ground-state radius, the first excited orbit is

options.B: 2 times larger

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: C. Since rn ∝ n², for n = 2 the orbit radius is 4 times the ground-state radius.

Atomic World.question: Excitation of an atom and ionisation of an atom are

options.B: both impossible for hydrogen
options.D: different: excitation raises an electron to a higher bound level; ionisation removes it from the atom

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: D. Excitation moves an electron to a higher bound level; ionisation removes it from the atom — different processes.

Atomic World.question: To ionise ground-state hydrogen, a photon must have

options.A: energy at least 13.6 eV; excess can appear as KE of the freed electron
options.B: energy exactly 13.6 eV only; any larger energy cannot ionise
options.D: energy equal to the Rydberg gas constant in joules

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. Ionisation needs at least 13.6 eV; any excess can appear as KE of the freed electron (energies above 13.6 eV still work).

Atomic World.question: If a photon’s energy exceeds the ionisation energy of an atom,

options.A: the atom absorbs only part of the photon and the same photon continues with the leftover energy
options.B: photons never interact with atoms
options.C: the atom can absorb the whole photon; ionisation occurs and excess energy can go to the electron’s KE
options.D: only elastic scattering of half the energy is allowed

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: C. The atom absorbs the whole photon; ionisation can occur and leftover energy becomes electron KE — photons are not partly absorbed and partly continued.

Atomic World.question: In Rutherford’s nuclear model, electrons

options.A: must fall straight into the nucleus because attraction has no orbit idea
options.B: are outside a tiny nucleus; classical orbits still had a radiation problem that Bohr later addressed
options.C: fill the entire atom uniformly like plum pudding
options.D: are inside the nucleus with the protons

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: B. Rutherford places electrons outside a tiny nucleus; classical orbiting still had a radiation problem that Bohr later addressed — electrons do not simply ‘fall straight in with no orbit idea’.

Atomic World.question: Most α particles pass straight through thin gold foil. By itself this observation

options.B: proves neutrons exist
options.C: proves electrons orbit in Bohr radii
options.D: fits both plum-pudding and nuclear models, so it alone does not rule out Thomson

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: D. Straight-through α tracks fit both models; large-angle scatters are what invalidate Thomson’s plum pudding.

Atomic World.question: A nanoparticle of a material

options.A: need not have a different shape; nano refers to size scale, not a mandatory shape change
options.B: must always have a different shape from the same material in bulk
options.D: must be exactly one atom across

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. ‘Nano’ refers to size scale; a nanoparticle need not have a different shape from the bulk material.

Atomic World.question: Resolving power and minimum angular separation: a higher resolving power corresponds to

options.B: infinite wavelength only

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: C. Higher resolving power means a smaller minimum resolvable angular separation θmin.

Atomic World.question: The energy of a photon emitted in a hydrogen transition equals

options.A: the electron’s total energy in the upper level alone
options.B: the difference between the two level energies involved
options.D: the Rydberg constant numerically in eV with no formula

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: B. Photon energy equals the difference |ΔE| between the two levels, not the electron’s total energy in one level alone.

Atomic World.question: Light’s wave–particle behaviour is illustrated by the fact that

options.A: interference needs waves while the photoelectric effect needs quantised photons — both can be true of light
options.B: light is only a wave forever
options.C: light is only a particle forever
options.D: photoelectric effect proves light has no frequency

Atomic World.explanation: Correct answer: A. Interference shows wave behaviour; the photoelectric effect needs quantised photons — both can be true of light (wave–particle duality).
